src: site, modelled on FA24 Exam 2, Q5A
stem:
Sodium isopropoxide and bromoethane give ethyl isopropyl ether in good yield. Sodium ethoxide and 2-bromopropane give very little of the same ether. Explain, with the mechanism of each reaction and the products that are actually formed.
[[rxn:CC(C)[O-].[Na+] + CCBr>>CCOC(C)C]]
[[rxn:CC[O-].[Na+] + CC(C)Br>>"very little ether"]]
model:
The reaction that works is {{SN2}}. The halide is primary. A lone pair on the isopropoxide oxygen attacks the {{CH2}} of bromoethane from the back and bromide leaves.

[[mech:sn2-isopropoxide-bromoethane]]

The reaction that fails is {{E2}}. Now the halide is secondary, so backside attack is slow (isopropyl 0.00083 against ethyl 0.033). Ethoxide is a strong base (ethanol has {{pKa}} about 16), so it removes a beta hydrogen instead.

[[mech:e2-2-bromopropane-ethoxide]]

The second flask holds mostly propene, ethanol and {{Br-}}, with only a little ether from {{SN2}}.

Lesson: the halide should be methyl or primary. The branched group goes in the alkoxide.

rubric.h: SN2 mechanism for the good route: O lone pair to the CH2 carbon, C-Br bond to Br, ether and bromide as products
Says the second halide is secondary, so backside attack is hindered and SN2 is slow
Says ethoxide is a strong base
E2 mechanism with three correct arrows: O lone pair to a beta H, C-H bond to C=C, C-Br bond to Br
Propene, ethanol and bromide given as the actual products (a little ether is acceptable)

steps.h: The oxygen carries an ethyl group and an isopropyl group. Pair 1: isopropoxide with bromoethane. Pair 2: ethoxide with 2-bromopropane.

ask.q: What is different between the two pairs?
ask.a: Only which piece carries the leaving group: a primary carbon in pair 1, a secondary carbon in pair 2.

steps.h: Bromoethane is primary; 2-bromopropane is secondary. The lecture rates are 0.033 and 0.00083, so backside attack is about forty times slower on the secondary carbon.

ask.q: Which carbon does the nucleophile have to reach?
ask.a: The carbon bonded to bromine. Its class decides, not the shape of the alkoxide.

steps.h: Both are strong bases: ethanol {{pKa}} 15.9, isopropanol 16.5. Wherever {{SN2}} is slow, a strong base takes a beta hydrogen instead.

ask.q: Is base strength what separates the two routes?
ask.a: No. Both alkoxides are strong bases. The halide is what differs.

steps.h: {{SN2}}, one step, two arrows: the oxygen lone pair goes to the {{CH2}} carbon from the side opposite bromine, and the C-Br bond goes to bromine. A primary halide with a strong base that is not bulky substitutes.

{{E2}}, one step, three arrows: the ethoxide lone pair goes to a hydrogen on a {{CH3}} of 2-bromopropane, the C-H bond becomes the C=C, and the C-Br bond goes to bromine. The hydrogen and the bromine are anti-periplanar.

steps.t: Write what is in the flask
steps.h: Propene (a gas), ethanol and {{Br-}}. The ethoxide has become ethanol: it is not part of the alkene.
Put the leaving group on the less hindered piece.

solution.answer: Isopropoxide with bromoethane: SN2 at a primary carbon gives the ether. Ethoxide with 2-bromopropane: a strong base with a secondary halide gives mostly E2 (propene, ethanol, bromide).
solution.rule: Williamson: methyl or primary halide, branched group in the alkoxide.

stem:
Sodium phenoxide and iodomethane give methyl phenyl ether. Sodium methoxide and bromobenzene give no ether at all. Explain, with a mechanism for the reaction that works.
[[rxn:[O-]c1ccccc1.[Na+] + CI>>COc1ccccc1]]
[[nr:C[O-].[Na+] + Brc1ccccc1>>COc1ccccc1]]
model:
Works: {{SN2}} at a methyl carbon. The phenoxide oxygen attacks {{CH3I}} from the back and iodide leaves. A methyl carbon is unhindered and has no beta hydrogen, and iodide is an excellent leaving group.

[[mech:sn2-phenoxide-iodomethane]]

Fails: the carbon that carries Br is {{sp2}}, part of the benzene ring. The back of the C-Br bond points into the ring, so a nucleophile cannot reach it: no {{SN2}} (the lecture rate for a leaving group on an {{sp2}} carbon is 0). An aryl cation is too unstable to form, so there is no {{SN1}} either. Bromobenzene is recovered unchanged.

Lesson: the ring must arrive already bonded to oxygen, as the phenoxide. The alkyl group is the halide.

rubric.h: SN2 mechanism: O lone pair to the CH3 carbon, C-I bond to I, methyl phenyl ether and iodide as products
Says why this is easy: methyl carbon unhindered, no beta hydrogen, iodide a good leaving group
Identifies the C-Br carbon of bromobenzene as sp2 (aryl)
Says an sp2 carbon cannot undergo SN2: backside attack is blocked by the ring
Says there is no SN1 either (aryl cation too unstable), so no reaction
Lesson: make aryl ethers from the phenoxide and an alkyl halide

steps.h: The oxygen carries a methyl group and a benzene ring. Pair 1: phenoxide with iodomethane. Pair 2: methoxide with bromobenzene.

ask.q: In each pair, what kind of carbon carries the leaving group?
ask.a: Pair 1: a methyl carbon ({{sp3}}). Pair 2: a ring carbon ({{sp2}}).

steps.t: Pair 1 is the best case for SN2
steps.h: A methyl halide can only substitute: rate 1 on the lecture scale, no beta hydrogen, no carbocation. Two arrows: oxygen lone pair to carbon, C-I bond to iodine.

{{SN2}} needs the nucleophile to come in exactly opposite the leaving group. On a benzene ring that side of the carbon is the inside of the ring. The lecture gives rate 0 for a leaving group on a C=C carbon; a ring carbon is the same.

ask.q: Where would the nucleophile have to stand for a backside attack on C-Br?
ask.a: Inside the ring, which is impossible.

steps.h: Ionization would put a positive charge on an {{sp2}} ring carbon. That cation is very unstable (lecture: vinyl gives no {{SN1}}), so it does not form.

ask.q: Phenoxide is a weaker base than methoxide. Does that matter here?
ask.a: No. Phenol has {{pKa}} 10, so phenoxide is a weak base, but it only has to attack a methyl carbon. The halide decides.

steps.t: What is in the second flask
steps.h: Bromobenzene and sodium methoxide, unchanged. Methoxide in methanol does not remove HBr from a benzene ring either: the product would need a triple bond inside a six-membered ring.
An {{sp2}} carbon can never be the electrophile of a Williamson synthesis. Bring the ring in as {{ArO-}}.

solution.answer: Phenoxide with iodomethane: SN2 at a methyl carbon. Methoxide with bromobenzene: the leaving group is on an sp2 carbon, so neither SN2 nor SN1 can happen and there is no reaction.
solution.rule: No substitution at an sp2 carbon: the aryl group must be the alkoxide.

stem:
Which pair of reagents is the best way to make benzyl tert-butyl ether?
[[mol:CC(C)(C)OCc1ccccc1]]

choices.why: The halide is primary and has no beta hydrogen (the next carbon is a ring carbon with no H), so even a bulky strong base can only substitute: {{SN2}}.
The halide is tertiary: no {{SN2}}. The alkoxide is a strong base and gives {{E2}}: 2-methylpropene, benzyl alcohol and bromide.
Two alcohols have no leaving group: {{HO-}} is a strong base and a poor leaving group, so nothing is displaced.
The bromine is on an {{sp2}} ring carbon, which cannot undergo {{SN2}}. The product wanted also has a {{CH2}} between the ring and the oxygen, which this pair does not contain.

steps.h: On one side of the oxygen is a tert-butyl group, on the other a benzyl group ({{CH2}} attached to a ring). The pairs are tert-butoxide with benzyl bromide, or the benzyl alkoxide with tert-butyl bromide.

ask.q: Which of the two halides is tertiary?
ask.a: tert-Butyl bromide. It can never be the electrophile of an {{SN2}} reaction.

steps.h: The carbon bonded to bromine is a {{CH2}}: primary. Its only neighbour is a ring carbon that carries no hydrogen, so there is no beta hydrogen to remove.

ask.q: tert-Butoxide is bulky and a strong base. Why does it not eliminate here?
ask.a: There is no beta hydrogen on benzyl bromide, so {{E2}} is impossible. Substitution is the only thing left.

steps.h: The benzyl alkoxide with tert-butyl bromide gives {{E2}}: 2-methylpropene and benzyl alcohol, no ether. This is the exam's failing route with a different alkoxide.
Two alcohols lack a leaving group. Bromobenzene has its bromine on the ring itself: wrong carbon, and an {{sp2}} carbon does not substitute.

ask.q: Benzyl bromide and bromobenzene both contain a ring and a bromine. What is the difference?
ask.a: In benzyl bromide the bromine is on an {{sp3}} {{CH2}} next to the ring. In bromobenzene it is on an {{sp2}} ring carbon.

solution.rule: The bulky piece is the alkoxide; the halide is methyl or primary, best with no beta hydrogen.

stem:
Which pair gives this ether in good yield?
[[mol:CCC(C)(C)OC]]

choices.why: The halide is methyl: unhindered, no beta hydrogen, {{SN2}} only. The tertiary group is safely in the alkoxide.
This puts the leaving group on the tertiary carbon. No {{SN2}} there: methoxide, a strong base, gives alkenes by {{E2}}.
This halide is primary and would substitute, but the oxygen ends up on the {{CH2}}: an isomer of the target, not the target.
Two neutral alcohols: no good nucleophile and no leaving group ({{HO-}} is a poor leaving group).

steps.h: The oxygen carries a methyl group and a tertiary group. Either the tertiary alkoxide attacks a methyl halide, or methoxide attacks a tertiary halide.
Bromomethane: methyl, {{SN2}} rate 1. The tertiary bromide: {{SN2}} rate 0.

steps.t: Check the product of each remaining choice
steps.h: A primary halide with the same carbons puts the oxygen on the wrong carbon. Two alcohols do not react.

solution.rule: Tertiary carbon on the oxygen side, methyl on the halide side.

stem:
A student tries to make tert-butyl methyl ether this way. What does the flask contain at the end?
[[rxn:CC(C)(C)Br + C[O-].[Na+]>CH3OH>"?"]]

choices.why: {{E2}}: methoxide takes a beta hydrogen and becomes methanol, the C-H electrons make the C=C, bromide leaves.
This would need {{SN2}} at a tertiary carbon, which does not happen: three methyl groups block the back of the carbon.
There is no water or hydroxide in the flask to supply an OH, and a strong base is present, so the halide does not wait to ionize.
Blocking {{SN2}} does not stop the reaction. The nine beta hydrogens are on the outside of the molecule, easy for a strong base to reach.

steps.h: Tertiary: no {{SN2}}.
Methoxide is a strong base (methanol {{pKa}} 15.5). Tertiary halide with a strong base: {{E2}}.
Base to H gives methanol. The C-H bond becomes the C=C of 2-methylpropene. The C-Br bond goes to bromine: bromide.

solution.rule: Alkoxide with a tertiary halide: E2, never an ether.

stem: Alkoxides are strong bases. With which halide is elimination impossible, whatever alkoxide is used?

choices.why: There is no carbon next to the C-I carbon, so there is no beta hydrogen to remove. Only {{SN2}} can happen.
Bromoethane has three beta hydrogens. It usually substitutes, but a bulky strong base can eliminate it.
Six beta hydrogens on a secondary halide: with an alkoxide, {{E2}} is the main reaction.
Nine beta hydrogens on a tertiary halide: with an alkoxide, {{E2}} is the only reaction.

steps.h: A hydrogen on the carbon next to the one that carries the leaving group.
Iodomethane has one carbon only. The other three halides all have beta hydrogens.
This is why the exam's good route used {{CH3I}} with the bulky alkoxide.

stem:
A student wants this ether and tries both pairs.

[[mol:COC1(C)CCCCC1]]

Pair 1: [[mol:CC1([O-])CCCCC1]] and [[mol:CI]]. Pair 2: [[mol:C[O-]]] and [[mol:CC1(I)CCCCC1]].

Which pair gives the ether? Give its mechanism. Say what the other pair gives instead: name the mechanism, describe its arrows and draw the major alkene.
model:
Pair 1 gives the ether by {{SN2}}. The oxygen lone pair attacks the methyl carbon from the back; the C-I electrons go to iodine.

[[rxn:CC1([O-])CCCCC1 + CI>>COC1(C)CCCCC1 + [I-]]]

Pair 2 gives no ether. The iodide is tertiary, so {{SN2}} is impossible. Methoxide is a strong base: {{E2}}. Three arrows: the methoxide lone pair takes an axial hydrogen from a ring carbon next to the C-I carbon, the C-H electrons form the C=C, the C-I electrons go to iodine.

[[rxn:CC1(I)CCCCC1 + C[O-]>>CC1=CCCCC1 + CO + [I-]]]

The major alkene is 1-methylcyclohexene, the more substituted one (Saytzeff). A little [[mol:C=C1CCCCC1]] forms when the hydrogen comes from the {{CH3}}.

rubric.h: Chooses pair 1
SN2 for pair 1: O lone pair to CH3, C-I bond to I, ether and iodide
Pair 2: the halide is tertiary, so no SN2
Methoxide is a strong base, mechanism named as E2
Three E2 arrows described or drawn correctly
1-Methylcyclohexene, methanol and iodide as the products
Gives a reason for the major alkene (more substituted) or mentions the minor one

steps.h: Iodomethane is methyl. 1-Iodo-1-methylcyclohexane has its iodine on a carbon with three carbon neighbours: tertiary.
A methyl halide can only do {{SN2}}. The tertiary alkoxide is bulky, but the methyl carbon is wide open.
Tertiary halide with a strong base: {{E2}}. The base takes a hydrogen from a carbon next to C-I: a ring {{CH2}} or the {{CH3}}.

Removing a ring hydrogen gives the C=C inside the ring with three carbon groups on it. Removing a methyl hydrogen gives a C=C with two. The more substituted alkene is the major product with a small base.

solution.answer: Pair 1 (the alkoxide with iodomethane) gives the ether by SN2. Pair 2 gives 1-methylcyclohexene, methanol and iodide by E2.
solution.rule: Tertiary halide plus alkoxide: E2, more substituted alkene.

stem:
This alkoxide, a single enantiomer with the (S) configuration, reacts with iodomethane in DMSO. What is the product?
[[rxn:C[C@H]([O-])c1ccccc1 + CI>DMSO>"?"]]

choices.why: The new bond is from oxygen to the {{CH3}} of iodomethane. None of the four bonds to the stereocentre is made or broken, so its arrangement is unchanged: still (S).
This applies inversion to the wrong carbon. {{SN2}} inverts the carbon that is attacked, which is the {{CH3}} of iodomethane.
A racemic mixture needs a planar carbocation at the stereocentre. Nothing leaves from that carbon here.
Elimination removes H and a leaving group from the halide. Iodomethane has no beta hydrogen, and the {{O-}} on the alkoxide is not a leaving group.

steps.t: Find the nucleophile and the electrophile
steps.h: The alkoxide oxygen attacks; the methyl carbon of {{CH3I}} is attacked.
O-{{CH3}} is made, C-I is broken. The C-O bond at the stereocentre is already there and stays.

steps.t: Apply the stereochemistry rule to the right atom
steps.h: Inversion happens at the methyl carbon, where it cannot be seen. The stereocentre keeps its four groups in the same arrangement.

solution.answer: The (S) ether: the configuration is retained.
solution.rule: A stereocentre on the alkoxide is untouched. Inversion belongs to the carbon that loses the leaving group.

stem:
Which pair gives ethyl phenyl ether?
[[mol:CCOc1ccccc1]]

choices.why: The halide is primary and phenoxide is a weak base (phenol {{pKa}} 10), so it substitutes: {{SN2}} at the {{CH2}}.
The bromine is on an {{sp2}} ring carbon: no {{SN2}} and no {{SN1}}. Nothing happens.
That ring is cyclohexane, not benzene. It is a secondary halide, and ethoxide would mostly eliminate it to cyclohexene.
Two neutral O-H compounds: no leaving group and no anionic nucleophile.

steps.h: Phenoxide with bromoethane, or ethoxide with bromobenzene.
Bromoethane: primary, {{sp3}}. Bromobenzene: {{sp2}}, which never substitutes.
A hexagon with alternating double bonds is benzene. A plain hexagon is cyclohexane, a different compound with a secondary carbon.

solution.rule: Aryl ethers: the ring is the nucleophile, never the electrophile.

stem:
A student plans to make tert-butyl isopropyl ether by a Williamson synthesis. Show that both possible pairs fail. For each pair, name the mechanism that takes over, describe its arrows and draw the products.
[[mol:CC(C)OC(C)(C)C]]
model:
The two pairs are isopropoxide with tert-butyl bromide, and tert-butoxide with 2-bromopropane.

Pair A. The halide is tertiary: no {{SN2}}. Isopropoxide is a strong base: {{E2}}. The oxygen lone pair takes a hydrogen from a {{CH3}}, the C-H electrons form the C=C, the C-Br electrons go to bromine.

[[rxn:CC(C)[O-] + CC(C)(C)Br>>CC(C)=C + CC(C)O + [Br-]]]

Pair B. The halide is secondary, and tert-butoxide is a strong base that is also bulky, so it is a poor nucleophile: {{E2}} again, with the same three arrows.

[[rxn:CC(C)(C)[O-] + CC(C)Br>>CC=C + CC(C)(C)O + [Br-]]]

Conclusion. A Williamson synthesis needs a methyl or primary halide on one side. This ether has a secondary carbon on one side of the oxygen and a tertiary carbon on the other, so neither pair works.

rubric.h: Writes both alkoxide and halide pairs correctly
Pair A: tertiary halide cannot undergo SN2
Pair A: E2 named, three arrows correct
Pair A products: 2-methylpropene, isopropanol, bromide
Pair B: secondary halide with a strong, bulky base gives E2; three arrows correct
Pair B products: propene, tert-butanol, bromide
Conclusion: neither side offers a methyl or primary halide

steps.h: One side of the oxygen is isopropyl (secondary), the other is tert-butyl (tertiary). Whichever side becomes the halide, it is hindered.
{{SN2}} rate 0. Any alkoxide is a strong base, so {{E2}} gives 2-methylpropene. The base leaves as isopropanol.

steps.t: Pair B: secondary halide, bulky base
steps.h: A secondary halide with an ordinary alkoxide already gives mostly {{E2}} (the exam's 2-bromopropane with ethoxide). A bulky alkoxide is an even poorer nucleophile, so the product is propene and tert-butanol.
The trap is assuming that one of the two routes must work. Check both before answering.

solution.answer: Both pairs give E2: pair A gives 2-methylpropene and isopropanol, pair B gives propene and tert-butanol. No ether either way.
solution.rule: No methyl or primary carbon on either side of the oxygen: no Williamson route.

stem:
Potassium tert-butoxide is to be turned into an ether. Which halide gives the best yield of ether?
[[mol:CC(C)(C)[O-]]]

choices.why: A methyl halide has no beta hydrogen and an open carbon. Even a bulky, strongly basic alkoxide can only substitute: this is the exam's good route.
Primary, but branched on the next carbon ({{SN2}} rate 0.003) and it has a beta hydrogen. A bulky strong base with a primary halide gives {{E2}}: 2-methylpropene.
A secondary halide with a bulky strong base gives {{E2}}: propene and tert-butanol.
The bromine is on an {{sp2}} carbon, which cannot undergo {{SN2}}: no ether.

steps.h: tert-Butoxide is a strong base (tert-butanol {{pKa}} 17.0) and a poor nucleophile because of its bulk. It will eliminate whenever it can.

steps.t: Ask which halide cannot be eliminated
steps.h: Only iodomethane has no beta hydrogen. (Bromobenzene cannot be attacked at all.)
The flowchart sends a primary halide with a bulky strong base to {{E2}}, and branching next to the carbon makes {{SN2}} slower still.

solution.rule: A bulky alkoxide needs a methyl halide.
